source.title: Rethinking Expert Trajectory Utilization in LLM Post-training for Mathematical Reasoning
source.authors: Bowen Ding; Yu-Han Chen; Jiayang Lyu; Ji-Yao Yuan; Qi Zhu; Shuangshuang Tian; Dan-Tong Zhu; Fu-Ting Wang; He-Yuan Deng; Fei Mi; Li-Feng Shang; Tao Lin

record.tranche_reason: The study examines post-training mathematical-task performance as SFT data scale and validation loss vary. This extends downstream-performance predictability to a post-training setting, but does not test the original pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports post-training accuracy ceilings, their relationship to SFT data scale, and correlations between minimum SFT validation loss and final performance. It does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws, extrapolation from small pretraining runs, parameter/token allocation at fixed compute, or architecture-shape effects.
record.test_reason: This is a post-training study of how to use expert trajectories (SFT, RL, synchronized SFT-RL) for math reasoning, and it does not test any version of the claim. The 'scaling' it measures is SFT data volume and SFT/RL compute in fine-tuning, not pretraining parameters, tokens or compute. Its loss predictor is SFT validation loss, not held-out pretraining loss. It fits no power law to loss: RL performance is fitted with sigmoids, and data-scale effects are reported as monotone ceiling comparisons over 5 datasets. Kaplan et al. is cited only for the FLOPs approximation (backward ≈ 2× forward). The record's V6 link stretches V6's 'scale or pretraining loss' to fine-tuning data scale and SFT loss. Those findings are related but are a different construct, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the paraphrase omits the first conclusion. The authors conclude that: (1) sequential SFT-then-RL beats pure SFT, pure RL and synchronized SFT-RL; (2) RL should start at SFT saturation (the Stable or Mild Overfitting regime by validation loss); (3) SFT data scale is the primary determinant of the ceiling, with trajectory difficulty acting as a multiplier; and (4) minimum SFT validation loss predicts the ceiling. They frame this as refuting 'Less is More'.
record.recipe_differences: Post-training experiments on mathematical reasoning using SFT and RL compute, validation loss, and benchmark accuracy; it does not implement the original pretraining loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute scaling recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance and ceilings vary with SFT data scale and difficulty, the SFT-to-RL transition point, and model initialization. The paper fits RL performance with sigmoid curves and uses robust fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Across SFT datasets, minimum SFT validation loss correlates strongly and negatively with the post-training math ceiling. On Qwen2.5-7B, Pearson r=−0.92 (Fig. 8a) and r=−0.94 over five scales (Table 5). On Llama3.2-3B, r=−0.96. Each correlation uses about 5 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning validation loss predicts the downstream performance ceiling reached after subsequent RL.

fits_no_version.finding: The post-training ceiling rises monotonically with SFT data volume: 77.3, 79.7, 82.6, 82.8 and 84.0 Apost for 1K to 889K samples on Qwen2.5-7B. Llama3.2-3B ranges from 25.0 to 70.4 max Ppost. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream accuracy after SFT-then-RL improves with fine-tuning data scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence is restricted to mathematical reasoning with R1-style expert trajectories; the authors state that generalization to other task types and trajectory styles remains open. Results do not address pretraining cross-entropy scaling.
record.rows_left_out: Other post-training paradigm comparisons, data-difficulty comparisons, and detailed SFT-to-RL checkpoint curves are not included because they concern post-training strategy or allocation rather than the downstream-predictability evidence recorded here.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small pretraining runs.
All: no parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.
No power-law fit of loss in fine-tuning or other regimes. The SFT data-scale effect is reported only as ceilings over 5 datasets, and RL is fitted with sigmoids.
No downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or pretraining loss. Model size (3B, 7B, 14B) is not treated as a scaling variable.
All: no comparison of pretraining exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: I disagree with the reader's 'tests V6 / T3'. Every scale and loss variable here belongs to post-training, not pretraining, and no power law is fitted to loss. The correlations rest on about 5 data points each. The Qwen2.5-14B transition-timing results (Table 6) are not recorded, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger pretraining runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study tests downstream mathematical-task performance predictability in SFT-then-RL post-training, not predictability from pretraining loss or across general downstream tasks.
Whether pretraining scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup and fitting choices, or whether pretraining curves depart from a single power law.
